title: Can a Memory Be Transferred — or Eaten?
hook: In the 1960s, scientists trained flatworms, ground them up, and fed them to untrained worms — chasing the wild idea that a memory might be a molecule you could pass along.
key_points: 1960s worm-training experiments suggested learning might transfer between animals, even by feeding.
The hope: memory is stored in a molecule like RNA that could be moved from one brain to another.
The results never reliably replicated, and the molecular-memory idea fell out of favor.
Modern neuroscience locates memory in patterns of strengthened connections between neurons, not a single substance.
content_html: In the 1960s, a series of worm-training experiments captivated the public — and some serious scientists. As Quanta Magazine columnist Claire L. Evans recounts, researchers trained flatworms to respond to stimuli, then asked a startling question: could that learning be passed on physically? Some experiments even ground up trained worms and fed them to untrained ones, testing whether a memory could literally be eaten.
extra_html: Behind the spectacle was a real and tantalizing idea: that memory might be stored in a single kind of molecule — RNA was a leading suspect — which could be moved from one brain to another. If true, learning would be a transferable substance. But the results proved slippery and never reliably replicated, and the molecular-memory hypothesis faded. As Evans's essay revisits, the episode is a vivid reminder of how seductive a simple answer can be. Today neuroscientists locate memory not in one magic molecule but in patterns of strengthened connections among many neurons — a picture explored in the Memory and Learning card.

related.title: Memory and Learning
related.hook: Every memory you hold is a pattern of connections between neurons — and learning is, quite literally, your brain rewiring itself to make those connections stronger.

related.title: Neurons and Signals
related.hook: Your every thought, twitch, and feeling rides on tiny electrical pulses fired by neurons — and leaps the gaps between them as bursts of chemicals.

flashcards.prompt: What was the strange hope behind the 1960s worm-training experiments?
flashcards.back_html: That a memory might be a molecule — something like RNA — that could be physically transferred from a trained animal to an untrained one, even by feeding.

flashcards.prompt: How does modern neuroscience say memories are actually stored?

choices.text: As patterns of strengthened connections between many neurons
As a single 'memory molecule' that can be eaten and absorbed
In one dedicated memory cell per fact

flashcards.explanation_html: The molecular-transfer idea never reliably replicated. Memory lives in patterns of synaptic connections across many neurons — not in a transferable substance.
